content: Splinter hemorrhages are small areas of bleeding that occur beneath the fingernails or toenails. These hemorrhages appear as thin, linear streaks of red to reddish-brown discoloration under the nails, aligned in the direction of nail growth. They are referred to as splinter hemorrhages because their appearance resembles a splinter lodged beneath the nail. In certain medical conditions, particularly infective endocarditis, small clots can dislodge from an infected heart valve and travel through the bloodstream to various parts of the body. When these clots reach the small blood vessels (capillaries) in the fingers, they can cause localized damage, leading to the formation of splinter hemorrhages. Splinter hemorrhages are not specific to a single disease and may be associated with a variety of conditions, including: Antiphospholipid syndrome Janeway lesions Psoriatic nail disease Rheumatoid arthritis Scleroderma Subacute bacterial endocarditis Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Physical trauma to the nails Trichinosis (a parasitic infection) The causes of splinter hemorrhages can be categorized as follows: Cholesterol embolization Infective endocarditis Psoriatic nail involvement Rheumatoid arthritis Scleroderma Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Nail trauma Trichinosis Vasculitis (inflammation of blood vessels) Over time, splinter hemorrhages undergo a natural progression in appearance. Initially, they are plum-colored, but within a few days, they darken to a brown or black hue. The presence of splinter hemorrhages is not a highly sensitive indicator of endocarditis, but it is relatively specific. Only about one in six patients with endocarditis will exhibit splinter hemorrhages. Therefore, the absence of these hemorrhages does not rule out endocarditis. However, if splinter hemorrhages are observed in a patient with clinical signs suggestive of endocarditis, this finding can be considered a fairly specific diagnostic clue. During a physical examination, particular attention should be given to the cardiovascular system, as splinter hemorrhages may be indicative of underlying circulatory or cardiac issues. Laboratory investigations may be necessary to support the diagnosis. These may include: Blood cultures to identify potential infections A complete blood count (CBC) to assess for abnormalities in blood cells Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) to evaluate for inflammation or infection
